paragraphs: I observed in the last chapter that the Americans have a less decided taste for general ideas than the French, and that this is especially true in political matters. The Americans put infinitely more general ideas into their legislation than the English do, and they pay much more attention than the English to adjusting the practice of affairs to theory. Even so, no political body in the United States has ever shown so warm an attachment to general ideas as the Constituent Assembly and the Convention in France. At no time has the American people seized on such ideas with the passionate energy of the French people in the eighteenth century, or shown the same blind confidence in the value and absolute truth of any theory. This difference between the Americans and the French has several causes, but chiefly the following one. The Americans are a democratic people who have always directed public affairs themselves. The French are a democratic people who for a long time could only speculate about the best way to conduct them. The social condition of France led the French to form very general ideas about government, while its political constitution kept them from correcting those ideas by experiment and gradually detecting their inadequacy. In America, by contrast, the two things constantly balance and correct each other.

At first sight this may seem to contradict what I said earlier, that democratic nations draw their love of theory from the excitement of their active life. A closer examination will show that the two statements do not conflict. People who live in democratic countries seize eagerly on general ideas because they have little leisure and because these ideas spare them the trouble of studying particulars. This is true, but it should be understood to apply only to matters that are not the necessary and habitual subjects of their thought. Merchants will eagerly take up, without very close scrutiny, any general ideas on philosophy, politics, science, or the arts that are put before them. But ideas that relate to commerce they will not accept without inquiry or adopt without reservation. The same is true of statesmen with regard to general ideas in politics. So if there is a subject on which a democratic people is especially liable to give itself up blindly and extravagantly to general ideas, the best corrective is to make that subject part of the people’s daily practical business. The people will then be forced to enter into its details, and the details will teach them the weak points of the theory. This remedy may often be a painful one, but its effect is certain.

So it happens that democratic institutions, which compel every citizen to take a practical part in government, moderate the excessive taste for general theories in politics that the principle of equality suggests.
